newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin sets targeted tax relief in budget.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin sets targeted tax relief in budget.

text.p: In his 1997/98 budget released on Tuesday, Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said he planned no personal tax increases over the next two years and proposed a set of tax cuts for poor families, charities, the disabled and university students.
"Our goal is straight forward. It is to reduce taxes," Martin said in his budget speech to Parliament.
He said the tax relief measures proposed on Tuesday would total C$2 billion in savings for Canadians over the next three years.
But he said a broad-based tax cut at this time would result in higher interest rates and would seriously reduce Canada's improved prospects for job creation and growth.
"Yes, there will be a time to consider a broad-based tax reduction," Martin said. "But we will not do it until we know we can afford it -- and until we know it can be sustained."

The 1997/98 budget proposed a C$600 annual increase in spending under the Canada Child Tax Benefit beginning in July 1998. Together with measures announced in the 1996 budget, this would increase spending on child benefits to C$6.0 billion annually.
Martin also proposed about C$70 million annually in increased tax assistance for people with disabilities.
He also offered increased tax relief for charitable donations by raising the amount of charitable donations which can be subject to tax credit to 75 percent of income for all charities.
The budget also proposed to reduce the income inclusion rate on capital gains from the donations of publicly traded securities to 37.5 percent from 75 percent.

Martin set new tax relief measures for students pursuing higher education and families saving for the education of their children. The finance minister proposed to extend the post-secondary education credit and double it over two years.

He proposed a doubling of the annual contribution to Registered Education Savings Plans, income from which is tax-free. Under the budget proposal, parents will be allowed to contribute up to C$4,000 a year and transfer unused funds into their retirement savings plans. ((Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau, 613-235-6745))
